documents.title: Cloud & Servers
documents.description: CloudHost247 cloud and servers: VPS, public and private cloud, dedicated and enterprise servers, operating systems, network, monitoring, firewalls and backups.

faqs.question: What is the difference between VPS, public cloud and private cloud?
faqs.answer: A VPS is a fixed slice of a shared machine with guaranteed resources. Public cloud is elastic compute that can be resized. Private cloud is capacity reserved for one tenant, so nothing you run shares hardware with anyone else.

faqs.question: Which operating systems can I install?
faqs.answer: The operating system catalogue page lists the families and versions the platform is configured to provision. It reflects configuration rather than a list of everything that technically exists.

faqs.question: Do servers include backups?
faqs.answer: Backups are a separate, explicitly scheduled job. Some plans include a backup allocation; where they do not, backups can be added to the service.

documents.body:
Cloud & Servers
Compute you can reach, size and operate
Virtual servers, cloud capacity and dedicated hardware — with the operating system catalogue, network controls, monitoring and backups that turn a machine into a service you can run in production.
• VPS and cloud instances
• Dedicated and enterprise hardware
• Operating system catalogue
• Monitoring, firewalls, backups
Call to action: Configure a server (/servers/new)
Call to action: See VPS plans (/hosting/vps)

Compute
Pick the shape of the machine
Each option is a different trade between isolation, elasticity and control.
• VPS Hosting — Guaranteed virtual resources with full administrative access, on shared hardware.
• Public Cloud — Elastic compute that can be resized as demand changes.
• Private Cloud — Isolated capacity reserved for a single tenant.
• Dedicated Servers — An entire physical machine, with no neighbour.
• Enterprise Servers — High-capacity configurations for serious workloads.
• Game Servers — Low-latency hosting for multiplayer communities.

Operations
Everything around the machine
A server without these is hardware. With them, it is a service.
• Operating Systems — The catalogue available at provisioning time.
• Infrastructure — Regions, facilities and how the network fits together.
• Monitoring — Telemetry and alerts on the resources you run.
• Firewalls — Rule-based network filtering per server.
• Backups — Scheduled jobs with a restorable history.
• IP Management — Addresses, reverse DNS and floating IPs.

What is on this page is what the platform can provision
Regions, operating system versions, control panels and machine sizes are configuration, not marketing copy. The platform lists exactly what a given deployment is configured to offer, and a service that is not configured is shown as unavailable rather than sold and then apologised for.
headings: Compute you can reach, size and operate

documents.title: Public Cloud
documents.description: Elastic public cloud instances from CloudHost247: resize compute as demand changes, with the OS catalogue, network controls and monitoring included.

faqs.question: Is public cloud the same as a VPS?
faqs.answer: They overlap. The practical difference is elasticity: a VPS is a fixed allocation, while public cloud instances are designed to be resized as demand changes.

faqs.question: Can I control the network at the instance level?
faqs.answer: Yes. Firewall rules apply per server, and the platform records the addresses assigned to your service.

faqs.question: Can I run more than one instance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Multiple servers can be provisioned and managed from the same account, each with its own operating system and configuration.

documents.body:
Cloud
Compute that changes size when your traffic does
Public cloud instances on shared, managed infrastructure — sized for the workload you have today, resizable when it is not enough.
• Resizable resources
• Wide OS catalogue
• Network and firewall controls
• Monitored host
Call to action: Configure an instance (/servers/new)
Call to action: Compare with VPS (/hosting/vps)

Why public cloud
Elastic where it matters
• Resize without rebuilding — Move to a larger or smaller instance shape as the workload changes, rather than migrating to a new product.
• Fast provisioning — Instances are created from a configured image, so a working server exists in minutes rather than days.
• Your choice of operating system — Provision from the catalogue of operating systems the platform holds images for.
• Network control — Firewall rules and private addressing so the instance is only reachable where it should be.
• Persistence — Attached storage survives a rebuild of the instance, which is what makes resizing safe.
• Monitoring built in — Resource telemetry is collected so capacity decisions are made from data rather than from an alert at 03:00.

This section lists the published plans and live prices for the catalogue product "public-cloud". Prices are read from the CloudHost247 catalogue at the time you ask; this page is the place to compare plan resources.
Live pricing
Public cloud instances on this deployment
Read from the product catalogue, so what you see here is what the order form charges.

Region availability is configuration, not a claim
A public cloud instance can only be created where the platform has a provider configured for it. The regions list on this deployment shows what is genuinely available; where it is empty, no region is configured and no instance can be promised.
headings: Compute that changes size when your traffic does

documents.title: Private Cloud
documents.description: Private cloud from CloudHost247: isolated compute capacity reserved for one tenant, for workloads that cannot share hardware with anyone else.

faqs.question: How is this different from a dedicated server?
faqs.answer: A dedicated server gives you one physical machine. Private cloud gives you reserved capacity that can be split across instances, with the boundary defined around your organisation.

faqs.question: Can I connect it to my office network?
faqs.answer: Connectivity options depend on the facility and the provider configured for the region. Raise the requirement with sales and the available options are confirmed in writing.

faqs.question: Is it multi-tenant under the hood?
faqs.answer: It is designed so that your workloads do not share resources with another customer's. The exact architecture depends on the provider and facility involved, and is documented for you before you commit.

documents.body:
Cloud
Capacity that belongs to one tenant only
Where a workload must not share a machine with anyone else, private cloud gives reserved resources and a defined boundary around them.
• Reserved, not shared
• Defined tenant boundary
• Your choice of OS
• Backed by dedicated hardware
Call to action: Discuss requirements (/contact)
Call to action: See dedicated servers (/hosting/dedicated)

The boundary
What isolation actually changes
• No noisy neighbours — Performance is not affected by another tenant's load, because there is no other tenant on the same resources.
• A smaller blast radius — Isolation is a security property as well as a performance one: there is no shared host to be reached through.
• Easier to explain — A defined boundary is far easier to describe in a compliance or customer questionnaire than shared hosting is.
• Your stack — Choose the operating system and configuration the workload needs, rather than working around a fixed image.
• Network under your control — Addressing, firewall rules and connectivity designed around the application.
• Managed if you want it — Operate it yourself, or have the CloudHost247 team run the platform layer for you.

This section lists the published plans and live prices for the catalogue product "private-cloud". Prices are read from the CloudHost247 catalogue at the time you ask; this page is the place to compare plan resources.
Live pricing
Private cloud capacity on this deployment
Read from the product catalogue, so what you see here is what the order form charges.

Private cloud is scoped, not self-service
Because the boundary has to be designed — capacity, region, network and operating system — private cloud is quoted against your requirement rather than sold from a fixed price list. The order flow starts with a conversation.
headings: Capacity that belongs to one tenant only

documents.title: Enterprise Servers
documents.description: Enterprise-grade server configurations from CloudHost247 for high-capacity workloads, with redundancy options, managed operations and provider-backed hardware.

faqs.question: Do you offer redundant power and networking?
faqs.answer: Facility-level redundancy depends on the provider and region. The available options are confirmed per configuration before ordering.

faqs.question: Can you monitor a cluster rather than one server?
faqs.answer: Yes. Multiple servers can be monitored from the same account, and the platform records telemetry per service.

faqs.question: Is there a managed option?
faqs.answer: Yes. Managed services cover the platform layer — patching, hardening, monitoring response and administration — alongside the server itself.

documents.body:
Servers
When a standard server is not enough
High-core, high-memory configurations for databases, virtualisation hosts and platforms that other services depend on — with the operational support to keep them running.
• High core counts
• Large memory footprints
• Redundancy options
• Managed operations available
Call to action: Discuss a configuration (/contact)
Call to action: See dedicated servers (/hosting/dedicated)

Sizing up
What changes at this level
• Sized to the workload — Configurations are chosen around measured requirements — core count, memory, storage throughput — rather than a fixed tier.
• Built for data-heavy services — The configuration that makes a database host viable: fast storage, memory for working sets, and cores for concurrency.
• A platform under other services — When a host runs virtualisation or containers, its failure footprint is larger — so resilience is designed in.
• Monitored as critical — Telemetry, alerting and capacity tracking so limits are seen before they become incidents.
• Managed operations — Patch management, hardening and hands-on administration available as part of the service.
• Backups and recovery — Backup jobs sized to the data volume, with a restore plan that has been agreed rather than improvised.

Quoted against requirements, not published as a price
Enterprise configurations depend on hardware availability, redundancy choices and region. Rather than publishing a price that cannot be honoured, enterprise servers are quoted against the requirement you describe.
headings: When a standard server is not enough

documents.title: Game Servers
documents.description: Low-latency game server hosting from CloudHost247 with the compute to hold a community, DDoS-path filtering and full administrative access.

faqs.question: Do you offer a one-click game panel?
faqs.answer: The platform provisions servers with the operating system and access you need. Where a specific game panel or a set of preconfigured game templates is not configured in your deployment, that is stated rather than implied.

faqs.question: Which games are supported?
faqs.answer: The server is general compute with full access, so it is not limited to a whitelist of games. What matters is the resources the game server needs — tell us and we size for it.

faqs.question: Is DDoS protection included?
faqs.answer: Network-level filtering and abuse mitigation are part of the platform. The specific capacity of that mitigation depends on the region and provider.

documents.body:
Servers
Low latency, high uptime, full access
Game servers live or die on two numbers: latency and whether the machine is up. Both come from infrastructure, not from a control panel skin.
• Full administrative access
• Network-level protection
• Choose your own game stack
• Backups for world data
Call to action: Discuss a game server (/contact)
Call to action: See VPS plans (/hosting/vps)

What a game server needs
The things that actually matter
• Latency first — Placement and network path matter more than raw clock speed. The region is chosen to sit near the players.
• Protection against floods — Game servers are a favourite target for traffic floods. Network-level filtering is part of the service, not an upsell.
• Full access — Root or administrator access, so you install and configure the game stack the way the community expects.
• Compute that holds a population — Player counts, plugins and world size drive requirements. Configurations are sized for the community you actually run.
• World data protected — Scheduled backups of the game data, because a corrupted world file is an unrecoverable community.
• Monitored — Telemetry on CPU, memory and network so a growth problem shows up before players notice it.
headings: Low latency, high uptime, full access

documents.title: Infrastructure
documents.description: How CloudHost247 infrastructure is organised: providers, regions, network, storage and the operational layer that runs customer services.

faqs.question: Where are CloudHost247 servers located?
faqs.answer: In the regions configured for your deployment of the platform, which are listed on the data centres page. That list is generated from configuration, so it cannot drift from reality.

faqs.question: Who operates the data centres?
faqs.answer: The facilities are operated by infrastructure providers. CloudHost247 operates the platform layer: provisioning, network configuration, monitoring, security response and support.

faqs.question: Can I choose a specific region?
faqs.answer: Where more than one region is configured, yes — region is a selection at provisioning time and is recorded on the service.

documents.body:
Infrastructure
The platform under the products
CloudHost247 runs customer services across facilities operated by infrastructure providers, with a control layer that owns provisioning, monitoring, DNS, certificates and backups.
• Provider-backed facilities
• Explicit region configuration
• Platform control layer
• Monitoring and reconciliation
Call to action: See available regions (/cloud/data-centers)
Call to action: Contact sales (/contact)

Architecture
How the layers stack
• Facilities and providers — Compute and network are delivered from data centres operated by infrastructure providers, chosen per region and recorded in the platform.
• Network — Public addressing, firewalling and private networking sit between the facility and your service, configured per server.
• Control layer — Provisioning, operating-system images, DNS, certificates, backups and monitoring are owned by the platform rather than by hand.
• Reconciliation — The platform continuously compares what it believes is provisioned against what the provider reports, so drift is detected rather than discovered.
• Observability — Server telemetry, service state and operation logs feed the same account view you use.
• Isolation — Services are separated at the platform layer, and access to provider credentials is restricted and audited.

Honesty
What this page will not tell you
• A list of cities — Regions exist only when a provider is configured for them. The data centres page shows what is genuinely configured in your deployment — no decorative world map.
• An uptime percentage — A published percentage that does not come from measured, customer-visible monitoring would be a number we invented. Service status shows what the platform can verify right now.
• Certifications we do not hold — Certification claims require an audit report with a name and a date. We publish none we cannot produce.

documents.title: Data Centers
documents.description: The data centre regions CloudHost247 is configured to deploy into, listed from live configuration rather than a marketing map.

faqs.question: Why are some regions missing?
faqs.answer: Because the platform is not configured to deploy there. Adding a region is an administrative configuration change, and it appears on this page as soon as it is configured.

faqs.question: Does CloudHost247 own the data centres?
faqs.answer: No. The facilities are operated by infrastructure providers. CloudHost247 operates the platform and the services that run on the hardware.

faqs.question: Can I deploy across more than one region?
faqs.answer: Yes, where more than one is configured. Multi-region architecture is designed per requirement — talk to us about what you are trying to achieve.

documents.body:
Infrastructure
Regions we can actually deploy into
This page lists the regions configured for this deployment of the platform. If a region is not configured, it is not offered — which is the only honest way to publish a locations page.
• Generated from configuration
• Provider named per region
• Region selected at provisioning
• Status shown per service
Call to action: Configure a server (/servers/new)
Call to action: See infrastructure (/cloud/infrastructure)

This section lists the data-centre regions this deployment is configured to deploy into, read live from the platform.
Available regions
Regions configured on this deployment

Selecting a region
What region choice affects
• Latency to your users — The physical distance between the facility and the people using the service is the single largest factor in response time.
• Data residency — Where data is stored is a legal question as well as a technical one. Region selection is how you answer it.
• The provider operating the facility — Each region names the provider that runs the physical site.
• Addressing and connectivity — IP ranges and the network path are determined by the region the service is deployed into.
headings: Regions we can actually deploy into

documents.title: Network
documents.description: The CloudHost247 network layer: public and private addressing, firewall filtering, reverse DNS, floating IPs and the observability that sits on top.

faqs.question: Can I get additional IP addresses?
faqs.answer: Yes, subject to the region and provider. Addresses are assigned to the service and are visible in your account.

faqs.question: Do you support private networking between servers?
faqs.answer: Where the provider and region support private networks, servers can be given private addressing that is not reachable from the internet.

faqs.question: Is there a bandwidth limit?
faqs.answer: The limit is the one stated on the product you bought. Anything described as unmetered still operates under the Fair Usage Policy.

documents.body:
Infrastructure
The path between your users and your service
Addressing, filtering, routing and the telemetry that tells you what is actually happening on the wire.
• Public and private addressing
• Rule-based filtering
• Reverse DNS control
• Traffic telemetry
Call to action: Manage IPs (/cloud/ip-management)
Call to action: See firewall rules (/cloud/firewall)

Capabilities
What you can control
• IP addressing — Public addresses assigned to your service, managed in your account, with the option to move a floating address between servers.
• Reverse DNS — PTR records set correctly, which matters for mail deliverability and for anything that logs connections.
• Firewall filtering — Rules applied in order to allow, deny or rate-limit traffic to a server, with the order visible.
• Flood mitigation — Known-abusive traffic patterns are filtered at the network edge rather than reaching the application.
• Traffic telemetry — Throughput and packet-level signals recorded per service so a change in behaviour is visible as a graph.
• IPv6 — Dual-stack addressing where the region and provider support it.

Bandwidth and traffic terms are contractual
Whether a service is unmetered, capped or burstable depends on the product you have, and the number that matters is the one on the plan you bought — not a figure on a marketing page. Where a fair-use expectation applies, it is written down in the Fair Usage Policy.
headings: The path between your users and your service

documents.title: Operating Systems
documents.description: The operating system catalogue available when provisioning a server on CloudHost247, including version lifecycles and provider image availability.

faqs.question: Can I install a custom ISO?
faqs.answer: Where the provider and region support custom images, yes. Availability depends on the underlying infrastructure provider.

faqs.question: Do you offer Windows Server?
faqs.answer: Windows-based services are available as products, and Windows images appear in the catalogue where licensing and the region allow.

faqs.question: How are end-of-life systems handled?
faqs.answer: They are marked in the catalogue so you can make an informed choice, and support will tell you if the version you are running has reached end of life.

documents.body:
Platform
Choose the base your service runs on
The platform holds images for the operating systems it can provision, tracks their lifecycle status, and shows availability per provider region — so you know what you will actually get.
• Version and architecture recorded
• Lifecycle status shown
• Per-provider availability
• Control panels where supported
Call to action: Configure a server (/servers/new)
Call to action: See control panels (/hosting/control-panels)

How the catalogue behaves
Facts the platform keeps track of
• Families and versions — Each entry is a specific family, version and architecture rather than a vague name.
• Lifecycle status — End-of-life operating systems are marked, because a server installed today should not be unsupported next year.
• Provider image availability — An operating system is only selectable where the provider in that region actually offers an image for it.
• Control panels — Where a panel is configured to be provisioned on top of an operating system, that mapping is explicit.
• Administerable — Versions, images and availability are configuration, maintained by administrators rather than hardcoded in the application.
• Supported means patched — Operating systems with active vendor security support are the ones worth provisioning; the catalogue shows which those are.

If a version is not in the list, it is not provisionable
This catalogue reflects what the platform is configured and able to install. A version that is not listed has no image configured for the selected region — we would rather show a shorter list than accept an order we cannot provision.
headings: Choose the base your service runs on

documents.title: Server Management
documents.description: Server management from CloudHost247: provisioning, operating-system lifecycle, monitoring, firewall control, backups, patching and hands-on administration.

faqs.question: Can you manage a server you did not provision?
faqs.answer: That depends on the provider and the access you can grant. Bring the details and we will confirm what is possible.

faqs.question: What counts as managed?
faqs.answer: The platform layer: operating system, runtime, monitoring, backups, firewall and response. Application-level administration and code changes are a separate engagement.

faqs.question: Do you support panels like cPanel or Plesk?
faqs.answer: Panels are provisioned where the platform is configured to install them, and the control panels page lists what is available rather than what is theoretically possible.

documents.body:
Operations
The work between a server and a reliable service
Provisioning is the easy part. Keeping a fleet patched, monitored, backed up and reachable — and knowing when something has drifted — is the job.
• Provisioning and lifecycle
• Monitoring and alerting
• Firewall and access control
• Backups and patching
Call to action: See managed services (/contact)
Call to action: See monitoring (/cloud/monitoring)

Available today
What the platform does for you
• Provisioning and rebuilds — Create servers from a catalogue image, rebuild them from a known-good state, and record which image each server runs.
• Access management — Administrative access is issued and rotated through the platform, and server credentials are stored encrypted rather than pasted into tickets.
• Monitoring and alerting — Resource telemetry collected per server, with alerting so a saturation event is noticed while it is still an event.
• Firewall control — Rules attached to the server, applied in a defined order, with the effective ruleset visible.
• Backups — Scheduled jobs with a run history and a restore path from your account.
• Reconciliation and logs — The platform compares desired state with provider reality and records every infrastructure operation for audit.

Managed services
Hand the platform layer to us
• Patching and hardening — Operating system and platform components patched on a schedule, with the changes recorded.
• Monitoring response — Alerts are acted on rather than merely delivered — the difference between monitoring and management.
• Incident handling — A named path for an incident: who is looking, what is being tried, and what customers are told.
• Change management — Changes made deliberately, with a way back, instead of directly on production at 17:55 on a Friday.
headings: The work between a server and a reliable service

documents.title: Monitoring
documents.description: Resource monitoring and service telemetry for CloudHost247 servers, applications and hosting, with historical data and alerting you can act on.

faqs.question: Can I see monitoring for a service I have?
faqs.answer: Yes — telemetry is attached to the service in your account, so the graphs for a given server appear with that server.

faqs.question: Do you alert me or fix it yourself?
faqs.answer: Both are possible. Standard monitoring notifies; managed services mean the alert is acted on by us as well.

faqs.question: Can I monitor something outside CloudHost247?
faqs.answer: The Tools Center includes network and DNS diagnostics that can check external endpoints from the platform.

documents.body:
Operations
Know before your customers do
Telemetry collected from the services you actually run, kept as history, so capacity planning is a data question and an incident has a timeline.
• Resource telemetry
• Historical trend
• Per-service scope
• Status page driven by real checks
Call to action: Open monitoring (/dashboard/servers)
Call to action: See service status (/status)

What is measured
Signals worth keeping
• Compute pressure — CPU and memory over time, so the difference between a busy day and a capacity problem is visible.
• Storage growth — Disk consumption trending, because a full disk takes a service down quietly and completely.
• Traffic — Throughput in and out, which is where a traffic spike or a leak is first detectable.
• Service state — Whether each service is reachable and answering, recorded as state rather than as a promise.
• Alerts that mean something — Notifications tied to a threshold rather than to every fluctuation, so an alert is worth reading.
• History — Retained telemetry you can go back through when working out when a problem actually started.

Why there is no uptime figure on this page
A meaningful uptime number has to come from independent, continuous, customer-visible measurement over a defined period. Anything else is a claim. The service status page reports the checks this platform can genuinely perform right now, and says plainly when something is not being monitored.
headings: Status page driven by real checks

documents.title: Server & Cloud Backups
documents.description: Backup jobs for CloudHost247 servers and applications: scheduled runs, visible history, defined retention and restores performed from your account.

faqs.question: How often do backups run?
faqs.answer: The schedule is per service. The job history in your account shows the runs that actually happened, which is more reliable than any statement about intent.

faqs.question: Can I take a backup right now?
faqs.answer: Yes. A manual run can be triggered before a change, and it appears in the same history as the scheduled runs.

faqs.question: What is the retention period?
faqs.answer: Retention differs by service and is stated in the Backup Policy, which is the authoritative document.

documents.body:
Data
Backups your services can be restored from
Scheduled jobs attached to the service they protect, with a run history and a retention period you can see — and a restore you can actually perform.
• Per-service jobs
• Visible run history
• Defined retention
• Restore from your account
Call to action: Read the Backup Policy (/legal/backup-policy)
Call to action: See hosting backups (/hosting/backups)

Mechanics
How jobs are managed
• Scheduled runs — Backups happen on a schedule attached to the service, not on someone's memory.
• Scoped per service — A server, an application and a hosting account each have their own backup record, so one restore never affects another.
• What a backup contains — Each record states what was captured — files, databases, volumes — so you know what a restore will bring back.
• Separate storage — Backup data is held on storage separate from the live service, so losing a server does not lose its backups.
• Restore path — Restores run against the service, with the selected backup shown before the restore begins.
• Failure visibility — A failed run is recorded as failed, which is the only way to know a backup plan is not quietly doing nothing.
headings: Backups your services can be restored from

documents.title: Firewalls
documents.description: Rule-based firewall control for CloudHost247 servers: ordered allow, deny and rate-limit rules applied at the network layer, with the effective ruleset visible.

faqs.question: Can I lock myself out?
faqs.answer: Yes — that is a real risk with any firewall. Platform-level console access exists for the servers that support it, and support can help recover access.

faqs.question: Is the firewall in front of the server or on it?
faqs.answer: Rules are applied at the network layer for the service, ahead of the application, and are managed from the platform rather than requiring you to edit rules on the host.

faqs.question: Does it protect against volumetric attacks?
faqs.answer: Network-level flood mitigation is part of the platform, but the capacity available depends on the region and provider. A firewall is a policy control, not a substitute for mitigation capacity.

documents.body:
Security
Close everything you do not need
Most exposed servers are exposed because a port was opened for one reason and never closed. Firewall rules make the intended surface explicit and reviewable.
• Ordered rules
• Allow, deny and rate-limit
• Per-server scope
• Effective ruleset visible
Call to action: Manage firewall rules (/dashboard/servers)
Call to action: See security (/cloud/security)

Control
What you can express
• Ordered evaluation — Rules are applied in sequence and the order is shown, because order is what determines the outcome.
• Default deny — A policy of closing everything and opening what the service needs is the one that ages well.
• Rate limiting — Limit connections from a source so a brute-force attempt or a runaway client cannot consume the service.
• Source restrictions — Restrict administrative ports to known addresses so SSH is not reachable from the whole internet.
• Per-service rules — Rules are attached to a specific server, so a change is scoped to the thing it was meant for.
• Auditable changes — Rule changes are recorded against your account, which makes an incident review possible.
headings: Close everything you do not need

documents.title: Cloud Security
documents.description: How CloudHost247 secures cloud services: credential handling, isolation, network control, patch management, logging and incident response.

faqs.question: Where are credentials stored?
faqs.answer: Provider and server credentials are encrypted at rest and are never included in API responses. Access is limited to the platform operations that need them.

faqs.question: Do you log administrative access?
faqs.answer: Yes. Administrative actions and infrastructure operations are written to an audit log in the platform.

faqs.question: Who do I contact about a security issue?
faqs.answer: Use the abuse and security route published in the legal and policy documents. Reports are handled under the Cybercrime and Abuse Policy.

documents.body:
Security
The controls behind the services
Credentials stored rather than pasted, access restricted and recorded, infrastructure patched on a schedule, and every operation logged.
• Restricted credential access
• Isolation by service
• Patch management
• Audited infrastructure operations
Call to action: Read security practices (/security)
Call to action: See the AUP (/legal/acceptable-use)

Controls
What is enforced
• Provider credentials — Infrastructure provider credentials are stored encrypted, never returned to a browser, and used only by the platform's own operations.
• Audit trail — Infrastructure operations and administrative actions are recorded, so who did what and when is answerable.
• Role-based access — Administrative capability is granted by role and re-verified server-side on every request rather than trusted from the interface.
• Service isolation — Customer services are separated so that one cannot read or control another.
• Patch management — Operating systems and platform components are patched on a schedule, with changes tracked against the service.
• Incident response — A defined path for detection, containment, notification and review — written down before it is needed.

Access you control
Protect your own account
• Turn on multi-factor authentication — TOTP and passkey authentication are supported. A password alone is the weakest link in any hosting account.
• Review administrative users — Staff and administrative access should be limited to people who need it, and removed when they do not.
• Keep recovery details current — Password recovery and second-factor recovery both depend on the contact details on the account being right.

documents.title: IP Management
documents.description: Manage the IP addresses assigned to your CloudHost247 services: public addressing, floating IPs, reverse DNS and the records that tie them to your services.

faqs.question: Can I get a dedicated IP for a website?
faqs.answer: Where the product supports it and the region has addresses available. Raise the requirement and the option is confirmed with the service.

faqs.question: Why does reverse DNS matter?
faqs.answer: A PTR record that matches the sending hostname is a deliverability signal for mail, and it makes connection logs meaningful for everything else.

faqs.question: Do addresses transfer if I move servers?
faqs.answer: A floating address can be reassigned within the same region. A change of region means a new address.

documents.body:
Infrastructure
Know which address belongs to what
Addresses assigned to services, reverse DNS that resolves correctly, and the ability to move an address between servers without asking support.
• Assigned and available addresses
• Reverse DNS control
• Floating addresses
• Addresses tied to services
Call to action: Open server management (/dashboard/servers)
Call to action: See network (/cloud/network)

Address management
What you can do
• See the assignment — Every address shows the service it belongs to, so an audit does not require a spreadsheet.
• Set reverse DNS — PTR records for your addresses, which mail servers and log correlation both depend on.
• Move an address — A floating address can be reassigned to another server, which is what makes failover practical.
• IPv6 where available — Dual-stack assignment where the region and provider support it.
• Justification for more — Additional address requests are assessed against real need, which is what keeps the pool usable for everyone.

documents.title: Managed Services
documents.description: Managed services from CloudHost247: patching, monitoring response, backup verification, firewall changes and hands-on administration, confirmed per plan.

faqs.question: Is management included with every server?

faqs.question: Can I take management on an existing server?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, if the operating system and application are ones we support. The team reviews the service first, because taking over a server nobody has documented is its own project.

faqs.question: Who is responsible when something breaks?
faqs.answer: We are responsible for the work in the agreed scope, and we will tell you plainly when a fault sits in your application rather than in the managed service.

faqs.question: Do you manage the application I installed myself?

documents.body:
Operations
The parts of running a server you would rather not do yourself
Management is an option on the services that offer it, confirmed in your plan or your proposal — not something we assume on every server we host.
• Confirmed per plan
• Patching and updates
• Alert response
• Backup verification
Call to action: Talk to the team (/contact)
Call to action: See server management (/cloud/server-management)

What management covers
Work we take over when it is in your plan
• Operating-system patching — Security updates applied on a schedule for the operating systems we support, with the maintenance window agreed rather than guessed.
• Monitoring response — Alerts that are not just sent but read: when a service you have management on goes down, the alert becomes somebody's job.
• Backup verification — Backup jobs watched and restores tested where the product supports them, because a backup nobody has restored is only a hope.
• Firewall and access changes — Rule changes and access troubleshooting carried out through the platform, so the effective ruleset stays reviewable.
• Hands-on administration — Service configuration, package installation from supported sources and the routine tasks a hosting panel exposes.
• A record you can read — Work is recorded against the service it changed, so you can see what was done and when without asking for a summary.

What management is not
Management does not include application development, custom code fixes, or 24/7 telephone response unless your plan publishes that. It does not cover third-party applications we do not operate, and it cannot promise that a service will never fail. Where a plan is silent on a task, the task is yours — and we will say so rather than let you assume it is included.

Confirm before you buy
• Which operating systems are supported
• What the maintenance window is
• Whether restores are performed for you
• What response times your plan publishes
• Which applications are in scope

How it starts
• Tell us about the service — The plan, the operating system and what the service has to do — a short description is enough to scope it.
• We confirm the scope in writing — What is covered, what is not, and the response expectation. This is the same scope a plan feature or proposal states.
• It becomes part of the service — Ongoing work is recorded against the service, and changes that need your consent are put to you before they happen.
headings: The parts of running a server you would rather not do yourself

documents.title: Application Deployment
documents.description: Operate supported CloudHost247 application installs and updates with deployment status, step events, per-application configuration and recovery where supported.

faqs.question: Can I deploy on every commit?
faqs.answer: Not through the core deployment queue: it does not watch Git repositories or run CI. A configured Git-enabled control panel may provide commit-triggered deployments; otherwise use your own CI and the supported platform API where available.

faqs.question: What happens if a deployment fails?
faqs.answer: The operation is recorded. The worker attempts to reverse completed infrastructure steps, but recovery of a previous application version depends on the operation and provider.

faqs.question: Are deployment logs kept?
faqs.answer: The deployment record keeps status, step states and event history. Source-build logs are available only if the selected Git-enabled panel provides them.

faqs.question: Can I use the same application in staging and production?
faqs.answer: You can create separate application installations with distinct configuration and domains, subject to the services and capacity available in your account.

documents.body:
Developers
A deployment you can inspect afterwards
CloudHost247 records supported application installs and updates against the services they change. Follow the deployment status and step events, then inspect the application configuration and recovery options available for that operation.
• Published application versions
• Recorded status and deployment steps
• Configuration per application
• Recovery where supported
Call to action: Browse applications (/apps)
Call to action: See environments (/developers/environments)

The deployment flow
What happens to a supported application
• Choose a published application — Select an application and version that the live marketplace marks as published. The native deployment flow uses that version’s stored manifest.
• Validate the target — The worker checks the application version, target server, supported hosting type and available capacity before provisioning.
• Provision and record — The deployment uses the configured image and resources, then records the operation status, step state and events against the installation.
• Review the outcome — Inspect the deployment record and application logs. If a supported infrastructure step fails, the worker attempts to reverse completed steps and records the result.

Properties worth having
What the deployment workflow records
• It is recorded — Each operation has a durable status, step states and event history rather than disappearing with a terminal session.
• Versions are explicit — Native deployments use a published application version and its stored manifest; an arbitrary repository commit is not implied.
• Configuration is separate — Application environment values are managed per installation; sensitive values are encrypted in storage and omitted from API responses.
• Failure is visible — A failed operation is recorded with its error and event history. The worker attempts to reverse completed infrastructure steps where it can.
• Scoped per application — Installations and deployment records are linked to the application and server they operate on.
• Tracked over time — The deployment history shows which supported operation ran and when.

Git builds and CI are separate capabilities
The core application deployment queue does not clone arbitrary Git repositories, run build commands or execute test suites. It deploys published application versions and their configured images. Git-based builds depend on a control-panel integration that is enabled for the selected service; check the live panel catalogue before ordering. Run tests in your own CI system.
headings: A deployment you can inspect afterwards

documents.title: Application Environments
documents.description: Configure CloudHost247 application environments: environment variables and secrets, persistent volumes, per-application domains and certificates.

faqs.question: Can I change a variable without redeploying?
faqs.answer: Configuration changes are applied to the application and take effect on the next release, so the running release always matches a recorded state.

faqs.question: Are secrets encrypted?
faqs.answer: Yes. Secret values are stored encrypted, are not returned to the browser after being saved, and are excluded from API responses.

faqs.question: What happens to volumes on redeploy?
faqs.answer: They persist. That is the point of declaring them: the container is replaceable, the data is not.

documents.body:
Developers
Configuration belongs outside the code
Environment variables, secrets, persistent volumes and the domain the application answers on — all attached to the application rather than committed to a repository.
• Variables per application
• Secrets not echoed back
• Volumes that persist
• Domains with certificates
Call to action: Open an application (/dashboard/apps)
Call to action: See deployment (/developers/deployment)

Configuration model
What lives on the environment
• Environment variables — Plain configuration values injected into the process, so the same image runs in different places with different values.
• Secrets — Sensitive values are stored encrypted in the platform, not shown again after saving, and never included in an API response.
• Volumes — Storage declared by the application so data survives a redeploy, a rebuild or a move between hosts.
• Domains — A domain can be attached to the application, with its own certificate, so environments are distinguishable at a glance.
• Service connections — Reference a database or cache the account owns instead of pasting raw hostnames and ports everywhere.
• Separate per environment — Staging and production are separate applications with separate configuration — the only way they can be safely different.

Practice
Things that keep environments sane
• Never commit secrets — If a credential is in the repository, it is in every clone and every backup of that repository. Rotate it once it has been.
• Keep environments structurally identical — The same services, the same variable names, different values. Divergent structure is what turns a staging pass into a false negative.
• Give the environment its own domain — An address that identifies the environment prevents the classic incident of debugging production while thinking it is staging.

documents.body:
Runtime
Node.js as a long-running service, not a script
A Node application is a process that has to stay up. The platform supervises it, restarts it when it fails, keeps its logs and routes a domain to it.
• Process supervision
• Environment configuration

• DNS and TLS in front
Call to action: View deployment options (/developers/deployment)
Call to action: See runtime options (/developers)

What the platform handles
The operational parts of a Node app
• Supervision — The process is managed and restarted after a crash, which is what turns a successful test into a running service.
• Configuration — Ports, connection strings and flags supplied as environment variables rather than edited into the source.
• Logs — Standard output and error are captured per application so an unhandled rejection is findable.
• Deployment — Native application deployments install published versions and configured images. Git source builds depend on an enabled control-panel integration.
• Data services — Managed MySQL-compatible, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis services your application connects to.
• Domains and certificates — Attach the hostname the service answers on, and let the certificate be issued for it.

Bring your own runtime discipline
The platform supplies the process management, isolation and observability. Dependency pinning, lockfiles, dependency audits and choosing a supported Node release remain the application's responsibility — and the ones that go wrong in production are almost always there.

documents.body:
Runtime
PHP that is patched, tuned and yours
A maintained PHP runtime with the extensions applications actually declare, plus the pieces a real PHP application needs: Composer, cron, OPcache and a database.
• Maintained runtime
• Composer available
• Cron scheduling
• Database and mail
Call to action: See hosting plans (/hosting/web-hosting)
Call to action: See Laravel hosting (/developers/laravel)

What a PHP app needs
Provided rather than assembled
• Maintained PHP — Runtimes that receive security updates, so an old version is a choice rather than an inheritance.
• Extensions and Composer — The extension set applications declare, and Composer to resolve dependencies from the lock file.
• Scheduled tasks — Cron entries for queues, imports and housekeeping, so the scheduled work a framework needs actually runs.

The honest part
PHP shifts responsibility to the application

• Use the lock file — Deploying without a lock file means deploying whatever the registry serves today — which is not the same thing as what you tested.

documents.body:
Runtime
Laravel with the parts that usually get forgotten
A Laravel application that works locally needs four things in production: a queue worker, the scheduler, writable storage and a database. All four are part of the hosting.
• Queue workers
• Scheduler cron
• Persistent storage
• MySQL or PostgreSQL
Call to action: Deploy Laravel (/developers/deployment)
Call to action: See PHP hosting (/developers/php)

Laravel specifics
The four things that break in production
• Queue workers — Supervised worker processes so queued jobs are processed and re-started after a deployment or a failure.
• The scheduler — A single cron entry running Laravel's scheduler, so you do not have to remember which tasks need which timing.
• Writable storage — Persistent volumes for uploads and framework storage, so a redeploy does not erase user files.
• Migrations — A database that can be dumped, restored and migrated with a backup taken before the change.
• Environment configuration — The values in .env supplied per environment instead of living in the repository.
• Logs — Application and queue output captured per service, which is where a failing job is actually visible.

Deploying a Laravel app
The sequence that avoids surprises
• Back up before migrating — Run the database backup first. A failed migration with no backup is a much worse day than a failed migration.
• Release the new code — Deploy from the repository so the release is tied to a revision rather than to a folder someone edited.
• Restart the workers — Queue workers must pick up new code; a supervised worker is restarted by the platform on release.
headings: Laravel with the parts that usually get forgotten

Runtime
If it runs in a container, it runs here
Build the image you want, run it on infrastructure you control, attach the volumes it needs and put a domain in front of it.
• Public and private registries
• Persistent volumes
• Environment configuration
• Domain and TLS
Call to action: See containers (/platforms/containers)
Call to action: See deployment (/developers/deployment)

Running containers
What the platform provides
• Image deployment — Run an image the platform can pull, so the tested artefact is the deployed artefact.
• Private registries — Registry credentials are stored so a private image can be pulled without embedding a token in a script.
• Volumes — State declared by the application lives on a volume, so replacing the container does not destroy data.
• Configuration — Environment variables and secrets applied per application, not baked into the image.
• Routing — Attach the hostname, let the certificate issue, and the container is on the internet the way you intended.
• Observability — Logs, resource use and restart behaviour recorded, so a crash loop is something you can see.

Container hygiene
Things that make containers safe to run
• Pin the tag — A moving tag means a redeploy can change the application without anyone deciding to change it.
• Do not run as root by default — A container that does not need root should not have it; privileged containers widen the blast radius for no benefit.
• Keep state on volumes — Anything written inside the container filesystem is temporary by definition, whatever it looks like during testing.
• Choose small base images — A smaller image pulls faster, starts faster and presents fewer packages to keep patched.
headings: If it runs in a container, it runs here

faqs.question: Are backups encrypted?

documents.body:
Data
A backup is only real if you can restore it
Scheduled backups with a job history you can inspect, a retention period you can see, and a restore path that has been thought through before you need it.
• Scheduled jobs
• Visible job history
• Per-service restore
• Documented retention
Call to action: See backup plans (/hosting)
Call to action: Read the Backup Policy (/legal/backup-policy)

How it works
What the platform actually does
• Scheduled, not manual — Backup jobs run on a schedule you can see, so protection does not depend on someone remembering to click a button.
• What gets captured — Files, databases and application data are captured according to the service, and each backup records what it contains.
• A job history — Every run is recorded with its status and size, so a silently failing job is visible rather than assumed to be working.
• Restore from your account — Restores are performed against the service they belong to, with the backup that will be used identified before it runs.
• Per-service scope — Each hosting account, server and application has its own backup record, so restoring one thing does not touch another.
• Stored separately — Backups are stored on storage separate from the live service, so losing the service does not lose the backup.

Say this out loud
What backups do not replace
• Your own copy of critical data — For anything you cannot afford to lose, keep an export you control in addition to platform backups.
• A tested recovery plan — Knowing what you will restore, in what order, is a decision backups cannot make for you.

documents.title: Website Migration
documents.description: Move your website and email to CloudHost247 with a planned cutover: copy, verify on the new infrastructure, then switch DNS at your discretion.

faqs.question: How long does a migration take?
faqs.answer: It depends on the size of the data and how the current host allows access. The copy and verification happen before any customer-visible change, and the DNS switch itself is decided by you.

faqs.question: Will my site be down during the move?
faqs.answer: The intent of the sequence is no downtime: the site is verified on the new infrastructure while the old one still serves, and DNS is the only change that customers can observe.

faqs.question: Can you migrate email as well as the website?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mailboxes and their contents are part of the inventory, and the MX records change at the same carefully chosen moment as the web records.

faqs.question: What if the migration does not work?
faqs.answer: Verification happens before the switch, so a failed migration is caught while the original site is still live. If the new platform cannot run the application, you keep the old host and we say so.

documents.body:
Hosting
Move your site without holding your breath
A migration is a sequence of small, reversible steps — copy, verify, then switch. The old host keeps serving until the new one has proved itself.
• We copy the files
• We copy the databases
• We verify before cutover
• You choose when DNS changes
Call to action: Start a migration (/contact)
Call to action: See hosting plans (/hosting)

The sequence
Six steps, in this order
• Inventory — We establish what is moving: files, databases, mailboxes, cron jobs, DNS records and any external service the site calls.
• Provision the target — The destination account or server is created and configured to match the application's requirements before anything is copied.
• Copy the data — Files and databases are transferred and the application is adjusted for the new path, hostname and connection details.
• Verify on a real hostname — The copied site is served on a temporary hostname and checked: pages resolve, forms submit, mail authenticates, the certificate is valid.
• Switch DNS — Only after verification, the domain's records are updated. Because the old host is untouched, this step is reversible.
• Confirm and tidy — We confirm the live site and mail behave, then the old copies and any temporary hostnames are removed.

What we need from you
Access to the current host, the domain's DNS control, and a list of anything the site depends on that is not obvious from the files — third-party APIs, scheduled jobs, unusual mail routing. Migrations go wrong when a dependency is discovered afterwards.
headings: Move your site without holding your breath

documents.body:
Security
Security that is operational, not a badge
Isolation between tenants, a patched platform, filtering ahead of your site, controlled access, and a documented response when something does go wrong.
• Tenant isolation
• Platform patching
• Abuse and malware filtering
• Auditable access
Call to action: See security practices (/security)
Call to action: Read the AUP (/legal/acceptable-use)

Layers
Where the protection actually sits
• Isolation between tenants — Accounts are separated at the service level so one compromised site is not a route into another customer's data.
• Platform patch management — The operating systems, runtime versions and platform components we control are patched on a schedule, not when someone complains.
• Filtering before your site — Known-malicious traffic patterns and abusive request rates are filtered at the platform edge, ahead of the application.
• Access control — Account access uses strong credentials, session controls and multi-factor authentication, including passkeys.
• Encryption in transit — TLS on every web endpoint and mail transport, with automated certificate renewal.
• Recovery and review — Security-relevant events are logged, and the incident path is documented so a response does not start from zero.

Shared responsibility
What is yours to own
• Your application's code — A vulnerable plugin or an injection flaw in your own code is not something the platform can patch for you.
• Your credentials — Weak or reused passwords on accounts you control are the most common route in, on any platform.
• What you publish — Content, scripts and third-party embeds you add to a site are your responsibility under the Acceptable Use Policy.

Platform
One application, one managed environment
Instead of sharing one runtime between everything you run, each application gets its own environment with its own configuration, logs and backups.

What you get
The pieces an application needs

Data
Databases as a service, not an afterthought
The database engines applications actually ask for, deployed as services that can be backed up, monitored and reached from the applications that use them.

Engines
What the platform deploys
• MySQL-compatible — The default for most web applications and content management systems, and the engine most hosting features assume.
• MariaDB — A MySQL-compatible engine where an application prefers or requires it.
• PostgreSQL — For applications that want stricter SQL semantics, richer indexing or extensions.
• MongoDB — Document storage for applications that model data as documents.
• Redis — In-memory key-value storage for caching, sessions and queues.
• Backups — Backup jobs scoped to the database service, so a restore brings back the data rather than the whole machine.

Managed means operated — it does not mean clustered
The platform deploys and can back up and monitor a database service. Automatic multi-node failover and read replicas are not claimed here; where a workload needs them, that is a design conversation about the infrastructure it runs on.

Platform
Bring the image you already build
If your application is already a container, it does not need rewriting to run here: run the image, attach the volumes it needs, configure it with environment variables, put a domain in front of it.

Containers here
How it works in practice
• Images — Deploy from an image reference the platform can pull, so the artefact you tested is the artefact that runs.
• Volumes — State lives on volumes declared by the application, so replacing a container does not destroy its data.
• Environment configuration — Configuration injected as environment variables, which is what makes one image runnable in several environments.
• Routing and TLS — Attach a domain to the container and certificates are issued for it.
• Logs — Container output captured per application, so debugging does not require shell access to a host.
• Resource visibility — CPU, memory and traffic recorded, so a container that is quietly restarting becomes visible.

What is not offered
There is no managed Kubernetes control plane on this platform, and no claim of cluster orchestration. Containers run as services attached to your account. If your architecture genuinely requires an orchestrator, that is a conversation about architecture rather than a checkbox.

A managed path from published app to service

The platform layer
What the native deployment flow handles

A real server, without a real server's commitment
Guaranteed CPU, memory and storage with administrator access, so you can install what the application needs instead of asking whether the host allows it.

What you get
The difference between a VPS and a share of one
• Guaranteed resources — Your allocation of CPU, memory and storage is reserved for your server. A neighbour's traffic peak is not your performance problem.
• Administrator access — Root or administrator access, so you install the runtime, the extensions and the services the application actually requires.
• Your choice of operating system — Provision from the operating-system catalogue, and rebuild from a known-good image if a change goes wrong.
• Network control — Firewall rules attached to the server, applied in a defined order, with the effective ruleset visible in your account.
• Backups — Scheduled backup jobs against the server, with a run history and a restore performed from your account.
• Monitoring — CPU, memory, storage and traffic recorded over time, so a capacity problem is a graph rather than a guess.

Choose carefully
A VPS expects you to operate it
• You own the operating system — Root access means the patching, the hardening and the service configuration are yours. That is the trade you are making for control.
• Or hand it over — Managed services cover the platform layer — patching, monitoring response and administration — without taking away your access.
• Not sure which size? — Start from what the application needs: memory for its working set, cores for concurrency, storage for its data. Support will size it with you.

VPS, cloud or dedicated
Pick by what you need from the machine
A VPS is a fixed allocation on shared hardware: predictable, economical, and the right answer for most applications that have outgrown hosting.,Public cloud adds elasticity — resize when demand changes instead of migrating. A dedicated server removes the shared hardware entirely, which matters when you need the whole machine's I/O or a defined physical boundary.

Why physical
When a VPS is not the right answer
• Undivided performance — Disk throughput, memory bandwidth and core count belong to your workload alone. That is what database and virtualisation hosts actually need.

Hardware detail is confirmed per configuration, not published as a guarantee

Most questions fall into one of four places: the documentation, a diagnostic tool, the knowledge base, or a ticket to the team. This page routes you to the right one.

documents.body:
Company
Security stated as practice, not as decoration
What we actually do to protect accounts, data and infrastructure — and what we deliberately do not claim, because a badge is not a control.
• Strong authentication
• Least-privilege access
• Encryption in transit and at rest
• Audited operations
Call to action: Report a vulnerability (/contact)
Call to action: Read the policies (/legal)

Controls
What is implemented
• Authentication — Password hashing with a memory-hard algorithm, multi-factor authentication by TOTP, and passkey (WebAuthn) sign-in as a phishing-resistant option.
• Least privilege — Role-based access for administrative functions, re-verified server-side on every request rather than trusted from the interface.
• Encryption — TLS for every public endpoint and mail transport, with certificates issued and renewed automatically; sensitive values encrypted at rest.
• Isolation — Customer services are separated, and provider credentials are held encrypted and used only by platform operations.
• Logging and audit — Authentication events, administrative actions and infrastructure operations are recorded, giving an answer to who did what and when.
• Response — A defined incident path: detection, containment, notification and review — documented before it is needed.

Disclosure
If you find a vulnerability
• Tell us, privately — Report through the contact route with enough detail to reproduce it. Do not test against another customer's service or data.
• We will acknowledge and investigate — Reports are triaged, and you get a response from a person who can act on it rather than an automated reply.
• Do not access data that is not yours — Proof of concept that stops at the boundary of your own account is welcome. Going further is not authorised, whatever the intention.

Certifications we do not claim
Where a compliance framework matters to you — ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA — ask, and you will get an accurate answer including 'not certified'. Publishing a certification we do not hold would be the single most damaging thing this page could do.
headings: Security stated as practice, not as decoration

CloudHost247 Isc: Privacy Policy Effective August 14, 2025 CloudHost247 Isc ("we," "us" or "CloudHost247.com") cares about protecting the personal information of our customers and visitors who use our websites, products, or services (collectively, our "Users"). This privacy policy provides details about how your personal information is collected, shared, and used by us. Information Covered by this Privacy Policy This privacy policy covers personal information, including any information we collect, use, and share from you, as described further below. This privacy policy applies to all CloudHost247.com websites, our products and services, and our mobile applications (collectively, the "Services"). This privacy policy does not cover how our Users may use or share data that they collect using our Services. When you purchase a Service from us, your personal information will be collected, used, and shared consistent with this privacy policy as well as any product-specific addendums related to particular services offered by CloudHost247 Isc, which are incorporated into this privacy policy. Information We Collect From You In the course of your use of the Services, we obtain the following information about you, as described below. We collect this data for the purposes described under "How We Use Your Information."

1. Signing Up for Services; User Information

Information you provide prior to any registration process, such as your email when you provide it to us.

Information you provide during registration (such as your name, company name, email address, phone number, billing address or credit card information, geographic location, and industry), when you contact us (for support or otherwise), or when you use our products or services.

Payment information you provide (via our Services or otherwise) when you purchase our products and services, including credit card data.

2. Use of Services, Website Visits, and Support

We collect data related to your online activity with our Services, such as:

IP address

Browser type and version

Geographic location

Pages viewed

Referral sources (how you got to our Services)

Links you click to leave our Services

Updates you make to your account

Metadata about your use of our Services (clicks, opens, etc.)

Interactions with videos or resources we provide

Support requests and issue reports

Device or other communication methods used

We store this data in system log files, backend databases, and analytics systems. Your telephone conversations with us may be monitored or recorded.

3. Social Media If you use your credentials from third-party social networking sites to log into some of our Services, we may receive information from those platforms (such as your name and email address to pre-populate forms). The specific information depends on your privacy settings with that social network.

4. Other Sources

Information provided at events or seminars.

Information from surveys.

Publicly available information.

Information you consent to share with us from third parties.

How We Use Your Information We use your personal information to:

Provide the requested Services.

Ensure the proper functioning of our Services.

Offer and improve our Services.

Provide technical support.

Facilitate navigation and usability of our Services.

Conduct advertising and marketing (with your consent where required).

Advertise third-party products/services (with your consent where required).

Diagnose technical issues.

Maintain security and compliance.

Administer our websites.

Personalize your experience.

We also use aggregated and anonymized data for reporting trends and statistics. Payment details are used only to process transactions. Recorded calls may be used for quality control and training.

Sharing of Information We may share your personal information:

With Partners to help you use our services, provide offers, or deliver relevant products (with your consent where required).

With Third-Party Vendors to assist with customer service, fraud prevention, analytics, advertising, hosting, and other operational needs.

For Corporate Transactions in the event of mergers, acquisitions, or sales of assets.

With Authorized Users such as account sub-users you grant access to.

For Legal Reasons where required by law, court order, or to prevent harm.

We will never sell your credit card or sensitive payment information.

Security While we take appropriate technical and organizational measures (including TLS encryption for financial data), no transmission over the Internet, email, or text can be guaranteed completely secure.

Tracking Technologies and Cookies We use cookies, web beacons, and similar tools for analytics, advertising, and service functionality. See our Cookie Policy for details and opt-out options.

Choice/Opt-out You can:

Opt-out of marketing emails via the unsubscribe link or by emailing privacy@cloudhost247.com.

Contact us to opt-out of marketing phone calls.

Manage cookies via your browser or our Cookie Policy.

Retention of Personal Information We retain your information for as long as necessary to provide services, meet legal obligations, resolve disputes, and enforce agreements up to seven years after account closure, unless otherwise required by law.

You're Rights (GDPR) Where GDPR applies, you have rights to:

Access: know what data we hold and how it's used.

Portability: receive certain data in a portable format.

Correction: fix inaccurate/incomplete data.

Erasure: request deletion under certain conditions.

Restriction: limit processing under certain conditions.

Objection: stop certain processing, including marketing.

Requests require identity verification and may be refused if legally justified.

Children Our Services are not intended for those under 18, and we do not knowingly collect data from minors.

Data Transfer Your data may be processed or stored in the United States or other countries outside your location, with safeguards to ensure compliance with privacy laws.

Notification of Changes We may update this Privacy Policy and will notify you via our website or email before significant changes take effect. Continued use of our Services after changes constitutes acceptance.

Contact Us If you have questions or concerns about this policy, contact us at: privacy@cloudhost247.com www.cloudhost247.com Last modified: August 14, 2025

Marketing Measurement Addendum

Effective upon publication of the CloudHost247 platform implementation, CloudHost247 uses a consent-aware Meta Pixel and, where configured, Meta Conversions API to measure website journeys and confirmed purchases.

Optional marketing measurement is off until you allow it in Cookie Settings. You may reject optional categories or withdraw consent later; withdrawal stops future browser and server marketing events for that choice.

Events may include the page path, product or plan identifiers, cart/checkout step, search result count, registration or contact completion, and a stable event identifier used to avoid double counting.

Purchase events are created only after a payment is confirmed and the related invoice/order is paid. Value and currency are taken from the payment record.

The default server payload contains a SHA-256 hash of an opaque consent-session identifier and, where available, Meta _fbp/_fbc values. It does not include your name, email address, phone number, password or payment-card data. Any future advanced-matching change requires separate review and consent.

Meta processes the data under its own terms and privacy policy. Marketing consent history is retained for up to 180 days, event activity for up to 90 days, and terminal delivery diagnostics for up to 30 days.

First-party Visitor Intelligence

When Analytics permission is explicitly granted and the feature is enabled by CloudHost247, the site may collect anonymous pageview and short-lived live-presence data for CloudHost247's own reporting. This is separate from GA4 and Meta, and neither service is used as its database or source of truth.

Data may include a random visitor/session/tab identifier, a sanitized origin-relative page path with query strings and fragments removed, a coarse referrer domain with subdomains removed, coarse device/browser/operating-system family, UTC timestamps and approximate country/region/city.

A network address is processed transiently through a verified server boundary for local GeoIP lookup and is not stored in Visitor Intelligence records. Coordinates are rounded city-centre estimates; no precise location or browser GPS is collected.

Visitor Intelligence does not store names, emails, account identifiers, passwords, authentication tokens, raw User-Agent strings, form contents or full referrer URLs. Admin browsing, automated crawlers and common health/uptime probes are excluded.

Visitor pageviews and session records are retained for a configurable period (90 days by default, adjustable from 7 to 365 days). Withdrawing Analytics permission stops new tracking and deletes visitor sessions and their linked pageviews for that consent record.

Questions or rights requests can be sent to privacy@cloudhost247.com.
